paras: The false report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey was a January 1882 newspaper story that a mob in Randolph County, West Virginia, had hanged a Black man named Luckey after he shot the white father of the woman he had married. First printed by the Wheeling Register and copied by papers from Virginia to Dakota, the story was called a lie by the Randolph County press within a week. Papers that had carried it then retracted it as 'wholly untrue' or contradicted it.

According to a special dispatch from Philippi dated January 28 and signed 'F.', a Black man named Luckey and a white woman named Collins, both of Randolph County, had married secretly in Maryland, 'the nearest Gretna Green'. The bride's father, a widower, was said to have been arrested shortly before after a failed elopement with a young woman named Kelly. A Register follow-up drawn from Randolph County men at the Capitol named the man Calvin C. Luckey, a young light 'mulatto', 'well known all over the county, and generally liked'.

In the Register's account, Collins visited the couple on Friday, January 27, to inflict 'condign punishment', and in the quarrel that followed Luckey drew a revolver and shot him dead. A 'crowd of hardy mountaineers' then overpowered Luckey, took him to the woods in front of the cabin and hanged him from a limb. The Capitol informants, who told the shooting 'so the story goes', believed Collins must have come at Luckey with a leveled rifle and attributed the lynching to local refusal to 'tolerate the inter-race marriage'.

A separate version, which the Oakland Republican traced to the Cumberland Times, said the couple had been refused marriage in Maryland and married at Wellersburg, Pennsylvania. In that telling Collins of Beverly sought them out, Luckey 'expected to be shot' and killed him, and a mob hanged Luckey to the nearest tree.

On February 6 the Wheeling Intelligencer reported that the Randolph Enterprise pronounced the Register's dispatch false, and it quoted the Barbour County Republican: 'There was no shooting or lynching at all, and nothing but a double elopement.' The Register itself noted that the Enterprise called the 'Becca creek lynching' a lie and said the Enterprise had been the innocent cause of giving it currency. The next day the Register defended its Barbour County correspondent, whom two Barbour men vouched for, saying he had passed on the story as it came to him and had no doubt of it at the time.
No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Register framed the story as a lesson about racial mixing, headlining 'Miscegenation in Randolph County Leads to Murder' and calling Luckey 'the assassin', though its follow-up judged him 'the better man' of the two. Distant papers cut it to crime-digest items: a Wisconsin weekly used a slur, a Dakota paper said he was 'lynched by a mob of white people', and an Iowa paper renamed him 'James Luckey', a farm hand of 'Thomas Collins'. The Maryland version circulated into March under the heading 'Marrying, Murdering, Lynching' in Minnesota and Dakota papers.

Correction travelled more slowly than the story; the Martinsburg Independent printed the Register dispatch as news on February 18, the same day the Morgantown New Dominion retracted its own reprint as 'wholly untrue'. The rival Wheeling Intelligencer used the denial to mock the Register's 'pretended dispatch', and the West Virginia Freeman said it was glad it had not published 'the Randolph county lynching yarn'.

The Register's Philippi dispatch and the Cumberland item both described a shooting and a lynching, but the two disagreed on where the couple married. Against them stood the Randolph Enterprise and the Barbour County Republican, which said only a double elopement had taken place. Because the Register's correspondent relayed what had come to him secondhand, the local denials are the closer evidence.

reader.title: False report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey
bases: A widely reprinted report that a mob in Randolph County hanged a Black man named Luckey after he shot his white father-in-law [A1, A2, A3] was called false by the Randolph Enterprise and the Barbour County Republican [A7, A8] and retracted or contradicted by other papers [A14, A18, A21].

The Register's correspondent described 'hardy mountaineers' hanging Luckey from a limb after he shot Collins [A1, A2], but the Randolph County paper called the lynching a lie and the Barbour County Republican said there was 'no shooting or lynching at all' [A7, A8]; the Register itself defended only its correspondent's good faith [A9], and no report confirms that anyone was killed.

Two apparently separate versions reported the lynching, the Register's Philippi dispatch [A1] and a Maryland item the Oakland Republican traced to the Cumberland Times [A3, A14], but the local Randolph and Barbour County papers denied it [A7, A8] and other papers retracted it [A18, A21].

accounts.label: Wheeling Register correspondent
accounts.gist: Luckey and Miss Collins married in Maryland; on Friday her father came to punish them, Luckey shot him dead, and a crowd of mountaineers hanged Luckey from a limb in front of the cabin.

accounts.label: Randolph men at the Capitol (via the Register)
accounts.gist: Luckey was a well-liked, 'respectable' man; Collins came at him with a rifle, and the mountaineers, who would not tolerate the marriage, hanged him; the shooting is told 'so the story goes'.

accounts.label: Maryland version (Cumberland Times, via other papers)
accounts.gist: Refused marriage in Maryland, the couple married at Wellersburg, Pa.; Collins of Beverly sought them out, Luckey 'expected to be shot' and killed him, and a mob hanged Luckey.

accounts.label: Randolph Enterprise and Barbour County Republican
accounts.gist: The lynching was a lie; there was no shooting or lynching at all, 'nothing but a double elopement'.

framing.detail: The Register headlined 'A Terrible Tragedy' and 'Miscegenation in Randolph County Leads to Murder', calling Luckey 'the assassin' while its follow-up called him 'the better man' and blamed the lynching on hostility to the marriage.
Distant papers condensed the story into crime-digest items, one using a slur and others headed 'Marrying, Murdering, Lynching'.
The rival Wheeling Intelligencer used the denial to mock the Register's 'pretended dispatch', and West Virginia weeklies called the story a 'yarn' and 'wholly untrue'.

info: Reported as Friday, Jan. 27, 1882 ('On Friday' in a Jan. 28 dispatch; 'last Friday' on Jan. 31); the event was later denied.
As reported, the woods in front of the couple's cabin in Randolph County; the Register later called it the 'Becca creek lynching'.
Reported victim: Calvin C. Luckey, a young 'mulatto' [A2]; 'James Luckey' in one digest version [A17]. Reportedly shot: Collins, the bride's father [A1], called 'Thomas Collins' in one version [A17].
As reported, Luckey shot Collins dead in a quarrel when Collins came to punish him for marrying his daughter.
As reported, 'a crowd of hardy mountaineers' [A1], 'the mountaineers of Randolph' [A2], 'friends of Collins' [A17], 'a mob of white people' [A16].
The Randolph Enterprise called the story a lie and said it had been the 'innocent cause' of its currency; the Barbour County Republican said there had been 'nothing but a double elopement'.
